source_prompt: Create a highly detailed, visually engaging, and scientifically accurate educational poster illustrating the chronological timeline of the discovery and the organizations or institutions involved in the discovery of the following chemical elements: Md (Mendelevium), F (Fluorine), Cl (Chlorine), Br (Bromine), I (Iodine), At (Astatine), Ts (Tennessine), Yb (Ytterbium), No (Nobelium), and He (Helium). Required Content Organize the elements according to their actual discovery dates, from earliest to most recent. For each element, include: Element Name and Symbol – Clearly display its complete name and chemical symbol. Discovery Date or Year – Indicate when the element was first discovered or identified. Discoverer(s) – Identify the scientist or research team credited with its discovery. Discovery Location – Mention the country, laboratory, university, or research facility where the discovery took place. Organization or Institution – Highlight the university, laboratory, scientific organization, or research institution involved in its discovery. Discovery Background – Provide a brief but informative explanation of how the element was discovered, synthesized, or isolated. Historical Significance – Explain why the discovery was important to the development of chemistry and the periodic table. Poster Design and Visual Presentation Use a chronological timeline layout, arranging all ten elements in the correct historical sequence. Make the timeline visually prominent, with clear dates, connecting lines, and distinct information sections for every element. Incorporate scientifically relevant illustrations, laboratory imagery, historical photographs of discoverers, and visual representations of the elements where appropriate. Use a distinct color scheme for each element while maintaining a consistent and professional overall design. Include small periodic-table-style element boxes containing the atomic number, chemical symbol, and element name. Use informative icons and visual markers to represent scientists, research institutions, laboratories, and discovery locations. Establish a clear visual hierarchy using bold headings, readable typography, organized text, and balanced spacing. Additional Requirements Ensure all historical information, discovery dates, scientist names, and institutional affiliations are factually accurate. Distinguish between the initial discovery, first isolation, synthesis, and official recognition of an element whenever these occurred in different years. For elements discovered through international collaborations, identify the participating research institutions and countries. Avoid overcrowding the poster while retaining meaningful scientific and historical details. Include a short introductory section explaining the importance of element discovery in the history of chemistry. Add a brief concluding section highlighting how scientific collaboration and technological advancement contributed to the discovery of these elements. Include credible references or sources at the bottom of the poster. Overall Style The final output should resemble a professional science exhibition or university-level educational infographic: visually attractive, historically informative, academically reliable, and easy to understand. Make the poster detailed enough for an academic presentation or classroom exhibit, with an engaging chronological storytelling approach that connects each element's discovery to the scientists, laboratories, and organizations responsible for advancing our understanding of the periodic table.

poster_data.title: ELEMENT DISCOVERY & PERIODIC-TABLE ORGANIZATION
poster_data.subtitle: 10 selected elements · from 1774 to 2009–2010
poster_data.intro: Element discovery transformed chemistry: from identifying substances in minerals and gases to detecting atoms made in laboratories.

items.label: Cl
items.title: Chlorine
items.detail: Scheele produced greenish-yellow chlorine by heating hydrochloric acid with pyrolusite. Humphry Davy later proved it was an element (1810).

items.label: I
items.title: Iodine
items.institution: Courtois’s saltpetre works and laboratory, Paris
items.detail: Courtois saw violet vapour while processing seaweed ash. Gay-Lussac later named the element after its violet colour.

items.label: Br
items.title: Bromine
items.detail: Balard identified an orange-red liquid in brine residues. Carl Löwig had independently produced a sample in 1825.

items.label: He
items.title: Helium
items.institution: Independent solar-spectroscopy observations; Janssen at Guntur and Lockyer in England
items.detail: Janssen and Lockyer independently detected a new yellow line in the Sun’s spectrum. Helium was isolated on Earth in 1895.

items.label: Yb
items.title: Ytterbium
items.discoverer: Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac · Geneva, Switzerland
items.detail: De Marignac separated a new oxide from erbium. The material still contained lutetium, which was separated in 1907.

items.label: F
items.title: Fluorine
items.institution: École supérieure de pharmacie de Paris
items.detail: Moissan isolated F₂ by electrolysing potassium bifluoride in liquid hydrogen fluoride after decades of dangerous failed attempts.

items.label: At
items.title: Astatine
items.discoverer: Dale R. Corson, Kenneth R. MacKenzie & Emilio Segrè · Berkeley, USA
items.institution: University of California, Berkeley Radiation Laboratory
items.detail: Bombarding bismuth with alpha particles produced this extremely radioactive element. Only tiny quantities can be made.

items.label: Md
items.title: Mendelevium
items.discoverer: Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg & Berkeley team · Berkeley, USA
items.institution: University of California Radiation Laboratory; 60-inch cyclotron
items.detail: Seventeen atoms were made by bombarding einsteinium-253 with alpha particles. Recoil separation enabled atom-at-a-time identification.

items.label: No
items.title: Nobelium
items.discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research team · Dubna, USSR
items.institution: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR), Dubna
items.detail: After disputed 1957–58 claims, Dubna achieved a conclusive synthesis in 1965. The early Swedish claim was later shown to be incorrect.

items.label: Ts
items.title: Tennessine
items.discoverer: JINR Dubna · Lawrence Livermore · Oak Ridge collaboration
items.institution: JINR U-400 cyclotron; Oak Ridge and Lawrence Livermore national laboratories
items.detail: Calcium-48 ions were fused with berkelium-249. IUPAC confirmed the discovery in 2015 and approved the name in 2016.

key_takeaways: Evidence matters: first observation, isolation, synthesis and official recognition can occur in different years.
poster_data.footer: Discovery advanced from chemical isolation and solar spectroscopy to accelerator-made nuclei through international collaboration.
poster_data.sources: Sources: Royal Society of Chemistry element histories · ACS Transuranium Elements at Berkeley Lab · IUPAC discovery and naming reports.
